title: What the labour-hour convention hid
bodyMd:
For most of the twentieth century, manufacturers assigned overhead — supervision, maintenance, scheduling, quality control — to products in proportion to the direct labour hours each product consumed. The convention made sense when it was adopted. Overhead was then a small fraction of total cost, and it genuinely did rise and fall with the size of the workforce. By the 1980s neither condition held. Automation had shrunk direct labour to a tenth or less of factory cost while enlarging the overhead pool, and much of that pool was driven not by hours worked but by the number of distinct products a plant handled: each additional item required its own setups, its own engineering changes, its own inspection routine.

The resulting distortion was systematic rather than random. Because overhead was spread over labour hours, high-volume products — which consume most of the hours but require proportionally few setups — absorbed most of the overhead, while low-volume specialty products absorbed very little of it. Reported margins therefore flattered exactly the products that were most expensive to make. Firms then responded to the signal as any rational manager would: they proliferated specialty lines that appeared profitable and, in several documented cases, surrendered high-volume products to competitors who were in fact producing them at a higher true cost.

Activity-based costing was devised to trace overhead to the activities that cause it, and where it has been implemented carefully it has reversed such judgements. But its record is uneven, and the reason is instructive. Assigning costs to activities requires estimates of how much of each activity every product consumes, and those estimates are supplied by the very people whose products are being judged. A costing system inherits the incentives of whoever provides its inputs — a limitation that no amount of methodological refinement removes.

The first paragraph explains that for most of the twentieth century overhead such as supervision, maintenance, scheduling and quality control was assigned to products in proportion to direct labour hours; that this made sense when overhead was a small fraction of total cost and varied with the size of the workforce; and that by the 1980s neither condition held, because automation had cut direct labour to a tenth or less of factory cost while the overhead pool grew and was driven largely by the number of distinct products, each needing its own setups, engineering changes and inspection routine. The second paragraph says the distortion was systematic: high-volume products absorbed most of the overhead because they consumed most of the hours despite needing proportionally few setups, low-volume specialty products absorbed very little, reported margins flattered the products that were most expensive to make, and firms consequently proliferated specialty lines and in several documented cases surrendered high-volume products to competitors whose true costs were higher. The third paragraph says activity-based costing was devised to trace overhead to the activities that cause it and has reversed such judgements where carefully implemented, but that its record is uneven because the estimates of how much of each activity a product consumes are supplied by the people whose products are being judged, so a costing system inherits the incentives of whoever provides its inputs.
